subChunks.title: Queries Inside Queries — Subqueries
subChunks.hookHtml: A subquery is a SELECT statement nested inside another statement. It lets you use the result of one query as input to another — without needing a temporary table.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Subquery in WHERE

-- Apprentices with above-average XP:
SELECT name, xp FROM apprentices
WHERE xp > (SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices);

The inner query runs first and returns a single value (a scalar). The outer WHERE uses it.

Subquery with IN

-- Apprentices who have completed at least one quest:
SELECT name FROM apprentices
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT DISTINCT apprentice_id FROM quest_completions
);

Subquery in FROM (derived table)

-- Average XP per rank, then filter for ranks with avg > 1000:
SELECT rank, avg_xp
FROM (
  SELECT rank, AVG(xp) AS avg_xp
  FROM apprentices
  GROUP BY rank
) AS ranked
WHERE avg_xp > 1000;

Subqueries in FROM are called derived tables. They must be given an alias.

Correlated subquery

-- Apprentices whose XP is above the average for their rank:
SELECT a.name, a.rank, a.xp
FROM   apprentices AS a
WHERE  a.xp > (
  SELECT AVG(b.xp) FROM apprentices AS b
  WHERE b.rank = a.rank   -- references outer query
);

A correlated subquery references the outer query — it re-runs for each outer row. Powerful but can be slow on large tables; CTEs or joins are often faster alternatives.

storyBeats.text: 'Show me apprentices with above-average XP.' One query — but the average itself must first be calculated.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: A subquery is a question inside a question. The inner one runs first, its answer becomes an input to the outer one. When the subquery references a column from the outer query — that is a correlated subquery. Powerful, but it runs once per outer row. On a million rows, that cost multiplies.

🏹 Solo

Return name for apprentices who have completed at least one quest (their id appears in quest_completions). Use a subquery with IN.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a correlated subquery is, why it can be slow, and when you might use a JOIN or CTE instead.

questions.prompt: A scalar subquery returns how many values?
options: Exactly one row and one column (a single value)
One or more rows, one column
questions.answer: Exactly one row and one column (a single value)
questions.explanation: A scalar subquery must return exactly one row and one column. If it returns more than one row, the query raises an error ('subquery returned more than one row').

questions.prompt: What does `WHERE id IN (SELECT DISTINCT apprentice_id FROM quest_completions)` return?
options: Rows where the apprentice's id matches any id in the completions table
Rows where the apprentice has completed every quest
Rows where the apprentice has completed no quests
All rows — IN with a subquery always returns all rows
questions.answer: Rows where the apprentice's id matches any id in the completions table
questions.explanation: IN with a subquery tests membership. A row passes if its id is one of the values returned by the subquery — i.e. the apprentice has at least one completion record.

questions.prompt: A derived table in FROM must have what?
options: The same columns as the outer SELECT
questions.explanation: All tables in FROM (including derived tables / subqueries) must have a name the outer query can reference. The AS keyword provides that alias.

questions.prompt: A correlated subquery runs once per outer row. Why can this be expensive?
options: If the outer query returns 1 million rows, the inner query also executes 1 million times — O(n) inner executions
Correlated subqueries always scan the entire table for each execution
The inner query cannot use indexes
Correlation requires a full outer join internally
questions.answer: If the outer query returns 1 million rows, the inner query also executes 1 million times — O(n) inner executions
questions.explanation: Correlated subqueries have N×M complexity where N is outer rows and M is inner cost. A JOIN or CTE often achieves the same result with a single pass. Use correlated subqueries when the correlated form is clearest; replace with JOINs if performance is critical.
